newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Indian minister ignores Bhutto call for conference.
newsitem.headline: Indian minister ignores Bhutto call for conference.

text.p: Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral dismissed a recently concluded Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) on Friday as a "half-hearted" arms control measure that legitimised the possession of nuclear weapons.

But, in a speech to the U.N. General Assembly, he made no mention of a proposal to the same body on Thursday by Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto for the convening of an international conference to resolve the long-festering Kashmir dispute with India and halt the danger of a nuclear arms race in South Asia.
Earlier, at a breakfast meeting with correspondents, Gujral said that, according to a 1972 agreement signed in Simla, India and Pakistan should settle their dispute over Kashmir bilaterally.
"We are not willing to change the format of the Simla agreement ... We cannot go outside that," he added.
In his speech to the U.N. Assembly, which did not mention Kashmir, Gujral said the security of India and of all countries "lies in a nuclear-free world."
"The only way to achieve this ultimate security is to ban production, possession and use of nuclear weapons within an agreed time-frame," he said.

"Partial and half-hearted measures of arms control, such as NPT (a 1970 Non-Proliferation Treaty made permanent last year) or CTBT, defeat this objective, by legitimising possession of nuclear weapons and permitting non-explosive testing of nuclear weapons by nuclear weapopns countries.
"India, therefore, cannot be a party to such flawed arrangements," he added.
Both India and Pakistan are believed to have nuclear weapons or the ability to assembly them quickly. India exploded a nuclear device in 1974 which it said was for peaceful purposes.

India's opposition to the CTBT recently prevented its adoption by the Geneva Conference on Disarmament, where decisions are made by consensus. It was brought instead to the U.N. General Assembly where it was overwhelmingly endorsed. But the treaty will not go into force until all 44 countries with nuclear reactors, including India, sign and ratify it.

Gujral appealed to the 185-member Assembly for support for India's bid for a seat on the Security Council for the two-year period 1997-98, citing its "unwavering commitment to the U.N., to the cause of multilateralism and our 50-year-long contribution to the maintenance of international peace and security."
India and Japan are vying for an Asian seat on the 15-nation council due to be vacated by Indonesia at the end of the year.
